tier_reason: Independent third-party suite ziyadedher/evm-bench (README table; runner code public in runners/evmone/runner.cpp and runners/geth/runner.go) shows evmone 66ms vs geth 235ms summed over five contracts; build type (CMake Release) and pinned versions are in the repo, but no compiler name and no CPU model are stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: evm-bench evmone runner: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (compiler not named), evmone 0.9.1 pulled via CPM; geth runner: `go run`, Go 1.19 module, go-ethereum v1.10.25
corrections.caveats: Evidence is the independent third-party evm-bench suite (ziyadedher/evm-bench, GPL-3.0, 225 stars, last commit 2024-03-19, renovate dependency bumps only). Its README states no hardware or compiler; the runners pin evmone 0.9.1 (Baseline interpreter, the default) and go-ethereum v1.10.25, both 2022 releases, so the table is several versions old. Each runner times only the contract call (deployment excluded), 5 runs per benchmark. The evmone runner executes against evmc::MockedHost (in-memory hash-map storage, fresh per run), while the geth runner goes through geth's full StateDB with access-list preparation and snapshot/revert on an in-memory database, so the storage-heavy erc20 rows charge geth for a state layer the evmone side mocks away; the compute-bound snailtracer row (43ms vs 163ms, about 3.8x derived from page data) is the fairest interpreter-to-interpreter comparison. Results are not cross-checked between runners beyond a success status. evmone's own geth-vs-evmone HackMD report (notes.ethereum.org, blocked here) was seen only as a search snippet: geomean evmone/Baseline 784M gas/s vs Geth 161M gas/s. The repo CHANGELOG has only self-comparisons (v0.9.0: Baseline 26% faster than 0.8.0 and 18% faster than Advanced on a 4.0 GHz Intel Haswell with Clang 15). The ipsilon/evmone repo was formerly ethereum/evmone.

notes: Numbers match the evm-bench README exactly (sums 66ms vs 235ms, relative 3.561x; per-row values correct). Shortcomings: no CPU or compiler stated, 2022 versions (evmone 0.9.1, geth 1.10.25), and an asymmetric host (evmone on evmc MockedHost vs geth on its full StateDB) that inflates the storage-heavy erc20 ratios; snailtracer gives about 3.8x. Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, 979 stars, 340 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-06.

tier_reason: Only vendor (block.one) marketing numbers from the EOSIO 2 announcement, seen as WebSearch snippets (medium.com blocked, eos.io no longer resolves); repo README, docs/OVERVIEW.md and the EOSIO v2.0.0-rc1 release notes carry no numbers. Vendor-blog evidence without methodology is C at most.

corrections.license: EOS VM License v1.0 (MIT-derived text with an added clause requiring source release of any covered work used for non-EOSIO blockchain purposes; not OSI-approved)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 7 stars, 18 forks on AntelopeIO/eos-vm; the original EOSIO/eos-vm has 200 stars, 62 forks; runtime of Antelope (EOSIO) blockchains
corrections.caveats: The repo README and docs have no numbers; the only bench tool (tools/bench-interp) prints parse and execution times without published results. The 16x/2x/6x claims come from block.one's EOSIO 2 announcement (Medium, blocked here; the eos.io copy no longer resolves) and the EOS VM Medium post, seen only as WebSearch snippets: 'EOS VM runs the EOS Mechanics WASM CPU benchmarks up to 16x faster than Binaryen'; WABT gave EOSIO 1.3 about 2x; EOSIO 2 up to 6x more (up to 12x faster than at launch). The snippet does not say which of EOSIO 2's three runtimes (EOS VM Interpreter, EOS VM JIT, EOS VM Optimized Compiler) produced the 16x; the Optimized Compiler (eos-vm-oc) lives in the EOSIO/Leap node repo, not here, so the figure may not apply to the code in this repo. The peer-reviewed 'VM Matters' paper (ACM TOSEM, arXiv 2012.01032; snippet only) measured EOS VM far slower than JIT/AOT engines on a matrix benchmark (one version: about 19,768 ms vs about 70 ms for WAVM and wasmtime; another: 21,855 ms vs about 170 ms WAVM and 156 ms wasmtime), so the win is only against the older Binaryen and WABT interpreters. Licence is the custom EOS VM License v1.0, not MIT: it adds a share-alike clause for use in non-EOSIO blockchain software, so it is not OSI-approved. AntelopeIO/eos-vm is the EOS Network Foundation continuation of EOSIO/eos-vm (its LICENSE says it is based upon EOSIO/eos-vm; GitHub does not mark it as a fork).

notes: Kept at C on snippet-only vendor numbers; shortcomings: no reachable numbers page, unclear which runtime (interpreter, JIT or optimized compiler) gave 16x, only beats old interpreters (Binaryen, WABT) and is far slower than wasmtime/WAVM per the VM Matters paper. License was wrong: the LICENSE file is the custom non-OSI 'EOS VM License V1.0', so usability moves to reference. Last commit 2025-07-30 (stale) confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party README Performance table; the benchmark programs for every language are in examples/asm/primes.asm comments, and the C++ row states G++ 7.3.0 -O3, but the CPU model is not named and the VM build used for the timing is not stated, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++ row: G++ 7.3.0 -O3; RISVM VM build per current repo Makefile: g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -O2 -march=native -fno-strict-aliasing -g (not stated whether this Makefile was used for the timing)
corrections.caveats: Toy-scale: one microbenchmark (trial-division primes below 100000, printing each prime) hand-written in RISVM register assembly versus idiomatic scripts, so it compares a low-level untyped 32-bit register bytecode with dynamically typed language VMs. The Lua 5.3 and Python 3.6.6 versions (in examples/asm/primes.asm comments) use global variables (Lua isPrime is global; Python runs at module level), which handicaps both baselines; Python loops to 100000 inclusive. Every run prints about 9,600 lines, so output cost is part of the timing. Versions (node 8.10, Python 3.6.6, Lua 5.3) are old and the machine is not named; the README itself says RISVM is about 3x slower than native and loses to node. Not compared with wasm3, WAMR, LuaJIT or any wasm runtime. The README warns there were no stack or bounds checks at the time (later commits added them).

notes: Numbers match the README and primes.asm exactly (RISVM 4.97s, Lua 5.3 7.23s, Python 3.6.6 35.95s; 1.45x and 7.2x derived correctly). Shortcomings: single toy benchmark, Lua and Python baselines written with globals, no CPU named, VM build flags not tied to the timing, abandoned since 2018-12-25. Metadata verified: MIT, 31 stars, 4 forks, not a fork.
